column1442: Install Low Flow Aerators - Kitchens and Bathrooms
column1446: During the site survey approximately 640 kitchen and 640 lavatory fixtures were identified with a flow rates of 1.5 gallons per minute (GPM) for kitchen fixtures and 2.2 GPM for lavoratory fixtures.  The standard flow rate for public lavatories is currently 0.5 GPM in lavoratories and 1 GPM in kitchens.  Reducing fixture water usage will not only save water and sewer costs but will also reduce energy consumption for domestic hot water production. Retrofit existing lavatory and kitchen sinks with low flow fixtures to reduce water use and lower domestic hot water costs. Retrofit is accomplished with a simple aerator replacement kit available from most plumbing supply houses that can be installed by in-house staff.

column1495: Linear fluorescent lamps, compact fluorescent, halogen, high pressure sodium, incandescent, and LED lamps were observed in common areas including the building lobby, stairwells, hallways, mechanical rooms, and exterior.  Replacement of the less efficient lighting types with higher efficiency LED lighting options will provide immediate energy savings and reduced operating costs.
column1539: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1544: Pinnacle Energy recommends evaluating this measure as an additional savings opportunity to the findings presented in this report.  A 157.77kW system will maximize available incentives and provide the best return on investment.
column1593: During the site survey approximately 640 showerheads were identified with a flow rate of 2.5 gallons per minute (GPM).  The standard flow rate for public lavatories is currently 1.5 GPM.  Reducing shower water usage will not only save water and sewer costs but will also reduce energy consumption for domestic hot water production. Currently, installation of low-flow aerators for showerheads is not economically feasible. However, if costs were to decrease in the future, it is recommended that management re-investigate retrofitting existing lavatory showerheads with low fixtures to reduce water use and lower domestic hot water costs. Retrofit is accomplished with a simple aerator replacement kit available from most plumbing supply houses that can be installed by in-house staff.  Costs shown are for installation of an aerator replacement kit.

column1544: The perimeter of Brooklyn Hospital is predominantly heated by fan coil units serviced by heat exchangers, which use boiler steam to heat the water distributed throughout the various hydronic heating systems. There are 13 heat exchangers throughout the hospital, servicing the OPD building, North Pavillion, West Pavillion, Power Building, and other areas. These heat exchangers are each serviced by pumps whose motors are standard efficiency past their useful life (15+ years). There are 20 pumps across all 13 heat exchangers, with varying motor sizes. There are eight (8) 7.5HP motors, five (5) 1HP motors, and seven (7) 3HP motors that provide perimeter heating hot water throughout the facility. Premium efficiency motors currently available would decrease the electricity used for pumping domestic water. It is recommended that NEMA premium efficiency motors be installed to replace the current motors.
column1593: The North Pavillion, Power Building, White Building, West Pavillion, and OPD Building are all older buildings with limited and inconsistent roof insulation. Space heating and is the single largest energy cost for all of these buildings and accounts for over 30% of all energy used. Weatherizing older buildings by improving roof insulation can significantly reduce your utility bills while providing a more uniform temperature within the building. In large buildings, it is common for warm air to rise vertically in the building and create a higher pressure on the upper floors. This warm air then leaks out on the upper levels while cold air flows in through cracks at lower levels to replace it. Because of this increase in pressure differenceâ€”known as the stack effectâ€”it is especially important to air seal and insulate the roof cavity. Install additional R-32 insulation in the roof cavities of the North Pavillion, Power Building, White Building, West Pavillion, and OPD Building and seal any air gaps and penetrations in the roof decks of each building.

column1446: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Install dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boilers.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 84% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, these dedicated units will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.

column1593: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment standalone radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the heating steam flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing steam flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing steam flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant.  Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1442: Insulate Pipes Less Than 3" In Diameter
column1446: During the site survey, un-insulated  domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter were observed in unconditioned spaces.  Un-insulated pipes in unconditioned spaces lead to significant thermal energy loss and cause related HVAC systems to operate with increased frequency and longer run times.  Insulating these pipes and all associated fittings in accordance with the New York City Energy Conservation Code (NYCECC) will minimize these thermal losses. Insulate all domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter in unconditioned spaces in accordance with the NYCECC.  All associated fittings such as elbows, valves, couplings, etc. experience heat loss and should be insulated as well.
column1490: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1495: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment steam radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the steam flow to the steam radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing steam flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing steam flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1446: Increase all cooling equipment setpoint. Each unit serving the common area is scheduled to maintain a setpoint temperature of 68 degrees Fahrenheit temperature, with the option of building manually changing the setpoint in case of a complaint. In this case during the Cooling season increasing thermostat dead band would allow the floor temperature to not change until it passes the 4-degree deltaT. This would allow for the temperature to increase up to 72 degrees. Calculations accounted for CDD above 72-degree Fahrenheit which resulted in electricity savings of 97,600.1 kWh with an associated cost savings of $ 19,520. The measure takes into account that the RTU and VRF heat pumps would operate for less hours.

column1495: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the steam flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing steam flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing steam flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant.

column1446: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Currently, installation of dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boilers is not recommended. However, if costs were to decrease in the future, it is recommended that management re-investigate installation of dedicated domestic hot water boilers. Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 80% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, this dedicated unit will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.
column1490: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1495: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment standalone radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the heating water flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing water flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing water flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant.

column1446: The heating and chilled water closed loop system is currently a constant flow system that operates continuously to supply  water to air handling and fan coil units throughout the building. Demand for heating and cooling water varies greatly based on the loads and occupancy of the building.  During unoccupied hours and shoulder seasons, most units will be bypassing water flow.  Although there is minimal need for heating and chilled water during these times, this type of system means that the pump is still circulating water at full speed.  This situation results in wasted pump energy during periods of low demand. Install VFDs on the closed loop water pump to optimize pump speed based on actual load conditions.  Any 3-way bypass valves must also be replaced with 2-way on/off valves on all air handling and fan coil units serviced by the closed water loop.  In addition, pump motors will need to be replaced with premium efficiency models as required for VFD compatibility.

column1593: The open condenser water distribution system is currently a constant flow system that operates continuously to supply condenser water to the building's cooling tower as a means of rejecting waste heat from the building's chiller. column1495: This measure is applied by installing insulated radiator covers with integrated temperature controls and sensors. An integrated radio in the cover communicates room and radiator temperature in real-time to centralized systems and instructs the system to provide heating only when necessary.

column1446: During the site survey, un-insulated domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter were observed in unconditioned spaces.  Un-insulated pipes in unconditioned spaces lead to significant thermal energy loss and cause related HVAC systems to operate with increased frequency and longer run times.  Insulating these pipes and all associated fittings in accordance with the New York City Energy Conservation Code (NYCECC) will minimize these thermal losses. Insulate all domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter in unconditioned spaces in accordance with the NYCECC.  All associated fittings such as elbows, valves, couplings, etc. experience heat loss and should be insulated as well.

column1544: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on tenant radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the steam flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing steam flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing steam flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1442: Insulate Pipes Less Than 3" In Diameter
column1446: During the site survey, un-insulated domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter were observed in unconditioned spaces.  Un-insulated pipes in unconditioned spaces lead to significant thermal energy loss and cause related HVAC systems to operate with increased frequency and longer run times.  Insulating these pipes and all associated fittings in accordance with the New York City Energy Conservation Code (NYCECC) will minimize these thermal losses. Insulate all steam pipes, condensate pipes, and domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter in unconditioned spaces in accordance with the NYCECC.  All associated fittings such as elbows, valves, couplings, etc. experience heat loss and should be insulated as well.

column1540: Install a Dedicated Domestic Hot Water Heater
column1544: In the summer, Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via an older, dedicated domestic hot water boiler that runs on fuel oil #2. This system is relatively inefficient as compared to newer, natural gas-fired DHW equipment. Install a dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boiler.  Fully condensing, natural gas-fired DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 80% for the current fuel oil-fired DHW boilers.
column1588: Low Cost and No Cost Recommendations
column1593: Two (2) 10HP motors [1 active, 1 standby] are used to provide domestic water pressure to the gravity tank on the roof of the building.  Three (3) 1.5HP motors are used to feed water back into the boiler. Four (4) motors (two 5HP, two 3HP) are used to power the vacuum pumps used with the steam & condensate system. These motors are standard efficiency motors that are past their useful life (15+ years).  Premium efficiency motors currently available would decrease the electricity used for pumping domestic water. Retrofit existing pump motors with NEMA premium efficiency motors. For all motors, premium efficiency motor converts more power input into useful work compared to a standard efficiency motor of this age.

column1490: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1495: The heating and chilled water closed loop system is currently a constant flow system that operates continuously to supply  water to air handling and fan coil units throughout the building.Demand for heating and cooling water varies greatly based on the loads and occupancy of the building.  During unoccupied hours and shoulder seasons, most units will be bypassing water flow.  Although there is minimal need for heating and chilled water during these times, this type of system means that the pump is still circulating water at full speed.  This situation results in wasted pump energy during periods of low demand. Variable flow water systems vary the pump speed in response to actual demand.  In these systems, bypass valves are replaced with 2-way (on/off) valves as needed and a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) is used to control the pump speed.  As air heating and fan coil units shut off and the 2-way valves close, pressure within the circulating system increases.  The VFD responds to this pressure increase by slowing the pump motor.  This reduction in motor speed provides significant energy savings.

column1446: During the site survey, un-insulated domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter were observed in unconditioned spaces.  Un-insulated pipes in unconditioned spaces lead to significant thermal energy loss and cause related HVAC systems to operate with increased frequency and longer run times.  Insulating these pipes and all associated fittings in accordance with the New York City Energy Conservation Code (NYCECC) will minimize these thermal losses.Local Law 87 Retro-commissioning requires that all chilled water pipes, steam pipes, condensate pipes, heating hot water pipes, and domestic hot water pipes 3" or greater be insulated in accordance with the NYCECC.  However, also insulating all pipes below 3" in size will provide reasonable energy savings.

column1593: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the steam flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing steam flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing steam flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Currently, installation of TRVs is not economically feasible. However, if costs were to decrease in the future, it is recommended management re-investigate the replacement of all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1544: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment hot water radiators. TRVs automatically regulate the heating water flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing water flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing water flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.
column1589: Install a Dedicated Domestic Hot Water Heater
column1593: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Currently, installation of dedicated DHW boilers is not economically feasible. However, if costs were to decrease in the future, it is recommended that management re-investigate the installation of dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boilers.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 84% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, the dedicated units will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.

column1446: Installing Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) on steam boiler radiators involves attaching TRVs to each individual radiator. TRVs function by sensing the temperature of the room and adjusting the flow of steam into the radiator accordingly. When the desired temperature is reached, the valve closes partially or completely, regulating the amount of heat emitted by the radiator. column1446: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Currently, installation of a dedicated DHW heater is not economically feasible. However, if costs were to decrease in the future as the efficiency of the boiler continues to decrease, it is recommended that management re-investigate installation of a dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boiler.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 84% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, this dedicated unit will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.

column1495: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment PTAC units. TRVs automatically regulate the heating water flow to the PTAC units based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing water flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing water flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1442: Insulate Pipes less than 3" in Diameter
column1446: During the site survey, un-insulated domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter were observed in unconditioned spaces.  Un-insulated pipes in unconditioned spaces lead to significant thermal energy loss and cause related HVAC systems to operate with increased frequency and longer run times.  Insulating these pipes and all associated fittings in accordance with the New York City Energy Conservation Code (NYCECC) will minimize these thermal losses. Insulate all domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter in unconditioned spaces in accordance with the NYCECC.  All associated fittings such as elbows, valves, couplings, etc. experience heat loss and should be insulated as well.

column1495: Linear fluorescent lamps, compact fluorescent, incandescent, high pressure sodium, and LED lamps were observed in common areas including the building lobby, stairwells, hallways, mechanical rooms, and exterior.  Replacement of the less efficient lighting types with higher efficiency LED lighting options will provide immediate energy savings and reduced operating costs.
column1539: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1544: Pinnacle Energy recommends evaluating this measure as an additional savings opportunity to the findings presented in this report.  A 10kW system will maximize available incentives and provide the best return on investment.
column1593: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons).Currently, installation of dedicated DHW boilers is not economically feasible. However, if costs were to decrease in the future, it is recommended that management re-investigate the installation of dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boilers.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 84% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, the dedicated units will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.

column1593: Combined Heat and Power (CHP) systems, also known as Co-Generation systems, provide on-site power generation via the combustion of Natural Gas in an engine or turbine that directly drives an electric generator.  This Electricity is utilized directly by the building to satisfy base electrical loads and, during power outages, is capable of providing emergency back-up capabilities.  In addition, heat from this combustion process is captured and may be used for domestic hot water production, and/or building heating.  It is this heat capture that greatly increases the overall efficiency of the system and results in cost savings as additional energy does not have to be expended for these domestic hot water and/or heating purposes.  These systems typically operate to satisfy only a portion of building electrical, heating, and/or domestic hot water loads and are therefore supplemental to traditional mechanical systems. The energy load profile and current system infrastructure at this building meets the prerequisite requirements for installation of a Co-Generation system, and further study is recommended. Preliminary analysis indicates that a Co-Generation system would provide significant energy cost savings at financially acceptable payback terms.  Further study is required to determine actual system feasibility and to provide an accurate assessment of implementation costs and energy savings.

column1446: During the site survey, un-insulated domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter were observed in unconditioned spaces.  Un-insulated pipes in unconditioned spaces lead to significant thermal energy loss and cause related HVAC systems to operate with increased frequency and longer run times.  Insulating these pipes and all associated fittings in accordance with the New York City Energy Conservation Code (NYCECC) will minimize these thermal losses. Insulate all domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter in unconditioned spaces in accordance with the NYCECC.  All associated fittings such as elbows, valves, couplings, etc. experience heat loss and should be insulated as well.

column1495: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the steam flow to the radiators and PTAC units based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing steam flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing steam flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1446: Cooling in this building is utilizing window AC units. Some of the tenants keep the AC units on the window during heating season. Heat escapes from the gaps at windows, over load the heating system and increase the heating cost directly. In addition, it create draft in the apartments and reduce the indoor comfort. We recommend remove all window AC units from windows during heating season. We understand that some window ACs may belong to tenants. If tenants do not want to remove them, installing window AC covers can be an alternative solution.

These light are on 24 hours per day seven days per week. Replacing the T-12 fixtures with high efficiency LED fixtures will result in substantial energy savings and peak load reduction. For example, the ArcLine 2ALN 2â€™ by 4â€™ Troffer LED Lamp fixtures are a competitive replacement for a lighting retro-fit. The fixtures have an input wattage of 20W or 40W with a 4,000 or 5,500 lumen output, respectively, depending on the package selected. The lamps are rated at 50,000 hours and come with a 5-year warranty. Each fixture costs approximately $132.

column1464: Based on field observations many units have high flow rate fixtures that can be upgraded. Replacing water fixtures with low-flowing fixtures is the most cost-effective water conservation measures. Aerating showerheads and aerators are inexpensive devices that can be installed to tenant units. These fixtures mix air with water, forming a misty spray. We recommend 1.5 gpm low flow aerators to kitchen sinks and bathroom sinks, and 2.0 gpm low flow showerhead to existing showers.

column1464: Based on field observations many units have high flow rate fixtures that can be upgraded. Replacing water fixtures with low-flowing fixtures is the most cost-effective water conservation measures. Aerating showerheads and aerators are inexpensive devices that can be installed to tenant units. These fixtures mix air with water, forming a misty spray. We recommend 1.5 gpm low flow aerators to kitchen sinks and bathroom sinks, and 2.0 gpm low flow showerhead to existing showers. The savings estimate assumes only the estimated percentage of the showers/sinks are replaced by low flow devices. The cost estimates are based on the time it will take for building staff to un-install existing showerheads/aerators, re-install new low flow devices, as well as repaire associated piping damage when needed.

column1446: During the site survey, un-insulated domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter were observed in unconditioned spaces.  Un-insulated pipes in unconditioned spaces lead to significant thermal energy loss and cause related HVAC systems to operate with increased frequency and longer run times. Insulate all domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter in unconditioned spaces in accordance with the NYCECC.  All associated fittings such as elbows, valves, couplings, etc. experience heat loss and should be insulated as well.

column1495: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the steam flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing steam flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing steam flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1495: This measure is applied by installing insulated radiator covers with integrated temperature controls and sensors. These systems allow for the control of heat energy transfer from the radiator to a room, while enabling feedback to the heating plant to optimize building-wide energy consumption. Each radiator cover incorporates a thermostatically controlled fan, which operates based on the room temperature set-point. An integrated radio in the cover communicates room and radiator temperature in real-time to centralized systems and instructs the system to provide heating only when necessary.

column1593: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the heating water flow to the radiator based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing steam flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing steam flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Currently, installation of TRVs is not economically feasible. However, if costs were to decrease in the future, it is recommended that management re-investigate replacement of all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1446: The corridor AC unit serving the common area corridors is an older unit, and is operating at reduced efficiency.  Direct replacement with a modern, high efficiency system would result in lower energy consumption, improved system reliability, and reduced overall operating costs. Capital replacement of this unit is not recommended at this time due to high implementation cost and long simple payback period.  However, if capital replacement becomes necessary due to ongoing maintenance issues, new equipment with premium efficiency ratings should be considered.  The incremental cost of premium efficiency equipment is directly offset by ongoing reduction in energy consumption.
column1490: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1495: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via hydronic boilers and indirect fired tank heaters.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Install a dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boiler.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 85% for the hydronic boilers.  In addition, this dedicated unit will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.

column1544: LED, halogen, linear fluorescent lamps, compact fluorescent, and high pressure sodium lamps were observed in common areas including the building lobby, stairwells, hallways, mechanical rooms, and exterior.  Replacement of the less efficient lighting types with higher efficiency LED lighting options will provide immediate energy savings and reduced operating costs.
column1593: Combined Heat and Power (CHP) systems, also known as Co-Generation systems, provide on-site power generation via the combustion of Natural Gas in an engine or turbine that directly drives an electric generator.  This Electricity is utilized directly by the building to satisfy base electrical loads and, during power outages, is capable of providing emergency back-up capabilities.  In addition, heat from this combustion process is captured and may be used for domestic hot water production, and/or building heating.  It is this heat capture that greatly increases the overall efficiency of the system and results in cost savings as additional energy does not have to be expended for these domestic hot water and/or heating purposes.  These systems typically operate to satisfy only a portion of building electrical, heating, and/or domestic hot water loads and are therefore supplemental to traditional mechanical systems. The energy load profile and current system infrastructure at this building meets the prerequisite requirements for installation of a Co-Generation system, and further study is recommended.  Preliminary analysis indicates that a Co-Generation system would provide significant energy cost savings at financially acceptable payback terms.  Further study is required to determine actual system feasibility and to provide an accurate assessment of implementation costs and energy savings.

column1446: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Install a dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boiler.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 80% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, this dedicated unit will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.

column1446: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the heating water flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing water flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing water flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1446: Existing Condition During the site visits it was observed that the former IKEA vacant sales floor was illuminated with nobody in the space. Per the building management system, the Lutron lighting control schedule for the cellar is 7AM-10PM. In addition, the sales floor lighting is monitored in real time on the BMS graphics. During the March site visit, the lighting scene was â€œMediumâ€ and the lighting actively consuming 25,892 watts. During the July site visit, the lighting scene was â€œHighâ€ and actively consuming 34,418 watts.    Recommendation  Lilker recommends the schedule is modified and lighting scene changed to reduce the energy consumption in the vacant space. The active schedule should be changed to reflect when the space is shown to potential tenants or when maintenance, cleaning, or other operations occur inside the space. In addition, during this time the lighting scene should be modified to â€œLowâ€ and special events in the scheduling can be added during showings or other occupied times to raise the lighting level to â€œHighâ€ when needed. For calculation purposes, Lilker assumed an adjusted occupied schedule of 9AM â€“ 5PM, and an energy consumption during the â€œLowâ€ lighting control scene of 10,000 watts.
column1455: Existing Condition The facility currently has all parking garage lights energized 24/7, even when fully unoccupied. This is resulting in unnecessary energy consumption during the night.  Recommendation  Lilker recommends implementing a bi-level lighting control strategy and installing occupancy sensors within the parking garage. This will allow for half the parking garage lights to de-energize at night, but still allow for override to full illumination by occupancy sensor activation if needed. When activated, the occupancy sensor will force all lights fully illuminated for 30 minutes, then de-energize half again if no other motion is detected. This will result in decreased energy consumption during occupied periods.
column1464: Existing Condition During the site visits, tenant lighting and base building lighting was evaluated. Several tenants including Old Navy, Burlington, and Marshalls currently have T8 fluorescent tubes installed. Recommendation  Lilker recommends all fluorescent lighting in the tenant spaces is replaced with LED equivalent bulbs. This will reduce energy consumption and resulting costs.

column1495: Existing Condition During the site visits, it was observed that the AHUs 1-5 serving the former IKEA space were existing to remain during the IKEA buildout. AHU-1 was noted to have a new 25 HP motor installed during the buildout. AHUs 2-5 have fan motors that may be reaching the end of their useful life. In addition, AHUs 2 and 5 are constant volume units, while AHUs 1, 3, and 4 have VFDs and operate as single zone VAV.   Recommendation  Lilker recommends retrofitting AHUs 2-5 with new NEMA premium efficiency fan motors. In addition, it is recommended to implement VFDs on AHUs 2 & 5 to operate them as single zone VAV to reduce energy consumption while space temperatures are satisfied.   This upgrade recommendation is contingent on a tenant taking over this space and assumed occupied hours of 7AM â€“ 10PM of a future retail store space. The energy and cost savings for this ECM is calculated based on these occupied hours and assumption that these AHUs exist to remain for the new tenant.

column1504: Existing Condition The 2-pipe HW/CHW plant at Rego Center 1 is constant volume, with three distribution pumps used. Pump-1 is hot water distribution and is 30 HP. Pump-2 is for chilled water distribution and Pump-3 serves the condenser water loop rejecting heat from the chillers and are both 50 HP. In both heating and cooling modes, a differential pressure setpoint is maintained by the bypass valve in the mechanical room.  Recommendation  Lilker recommends retrofitting the central plant pumps with VFDs for variable volume operation. To reduce the speed of the building pumps while maintaining required flow through the chillers and boiler, a primary boiler pump and two primary chilled water pumps are recommended to be installed. In addition, 2-way HW/CHW valves at AHUs 1-8 in the vacant ground and second floor spaces will need to be installed for proper variable volume operation. Variable volume control will allow for reducing speed of the pumps when allowed based on closing of the valves at AHUs when heating and cooling is not needed. This will result in reduced energy consumption and longer useful lifetime of the pumps.  Since the existing constant volume pumps are on the return side of the boiler/chillers, re-piping in the mechanical room will have to occur to modify the HW/CHW pumps to be on the secondary distribution to the building loop.  This upgrade recommendation is contingent on tenants taking over the ground and second level vacant spaces where the HW/CHW 2-pipe system serves. The energy and cost savings for this ECM is calculated based on assumed occupied hours of 7AM â€“ 10PM for the new tenant space, as well as the existing AHUs 1-8 remaining with proper unoccupied temperature setbacks.
column1513: Existing Conditions: The existing boiler at the facility is a sectional Well-McLain 2194 boiler. The combustion efficiency of the natural gas fired burner is 70%, and due to the age of the equipment, the total operating efficiency is most likely lower. In addition, the current boiler has a long off cycle delay, and is minimally controlled/monitored through the BMS.  Recommendation: Lilker recommends replacing the existing boiler with two high efficiency, condensing natural gas boilers. Similar capacity condensing boilers (5000 MBH) have combustion efficiencies up to 96%. Lilker recommends installing two boilers for redundancy and extra capacity if needed in the future. The new boilers should be fully integrated and controlled by the BMS. This upgrade recommendation is contingent on tenants taking over the ground and second level vacant spaces where the HW/CHW 2-pipe system serves. The energy and cost savings for this ECM is calculated based on assumed occupied hours of 7AM â€“ 10PM for the new tenant space, as well as the existing AHUs 1-8 remaining with proper unoccupied temperature setbacks.

column1544: Existing Condition During the site assessment, Lilker observed that the top level of the parking garage receives a lot of sunlight during the day. The rooftop of the facility does not have a singular large open area for a solar opportunity due to rooftop ductwork, RTUs, various fans, and other equipment spread across it.   Recommendation  Lilker recommends installing a solar canopy over the rows of spots on the top level of the parking garage. In addition to helping generate electricity for the facility, this will improve the parking experience by providing shade in the summer for shoppers intending to enter the third level Burlington, Old Navy, and Bed, Bath, & Beyond.   Lilker utilized the National Renewable Energy Laboratory PVWatts platform to calculate the annual electric production for the solar parking canopy. The area that the canopy would cover is estimated in the figure below. System losses and inefficiencies are calculated by defaults and user inputs into the platform. The assumptions and monthly energy production estimates are detailed in Appendix C.
column1553: Existing Condition The facility currently utilizes natural gas for most heating needs. The existing boiler is natural gas fired and tenant RTUs (Except Old Navy) utilize natural gas heating. In addition, some unit heaters for the base building (mechanical penthouse) utilize natural gas heating. The boiler is reaching the end of its useful life and is very inefficient. The tenant RTUs are at varying ages and conditions. As a result of Local Law 97 and greenhouse gas emissions associated with burning fossil fuels, as well as the electric grid planning to become more sustainable and cleaner in the future, fossil fuels consumption is planned to be greatly reduced in New York City buildings. Recommendation  Lilker recommends the following steps to convert the HVAC systems at the facility to fully operate on electricity via a water source heat pump system: â€¢	Demolish electric chillers â€¢	Demolish and replace existing boiler with electric resistance or heat pump electric boilers for heat injection to the new water source heat pump system â€¢	Utilize existing cooling towers for heat rejection from the water source heat pump system. Add additional cooling towers as needed to match the cooling needs for addition of WSHP RTUs.  â€¢	Demolish existing pumps and associated 2-pipe CHW/HW piping in the mechanical room. â€¢	Utilize existing condenser water piping and connect to new heat exchangers in the mechanical penthouse to separate the open condenser water loop from the heat pump loop (one per tower). â€¢	Install primary condenser water pumps on the open condenser loop (one per tower). â€¢	Once a tenant(s) has been found for the vacant ground and 2nd level spaces, demolish AHU-1 through AHU-8 and replace with water source heat pumps with 2-way valves as sized for the new tenant(s). â€¢	As Old Navy, Marshalls, Bed Bath & Beyond, and Burlington RTUs fail or reach the end of their useful life, replace with water source heat pump RTUs with 2-way valves, enthalpy wheels, and economizer controls. Install additional cooling towers, heat exchangers, primary condenser water pumps, and electric resistance / electric heat pump boilers as needed for the increased capacity.  â€¢	Install variable volume heat pump loop pumps for distribution to the WSHPs and water-source RTUs.  The following is assumed for the purposes of the ECM. The building owner should confirm the following assumptions or deviations from the assumptions are taken into account in any study / further analysis of this ECM:   â€¢	All WSHPs replacing AHUs 1-8 are variable volume serving VAVs with electric reheat.  â€¢	All currently CAV RTUs for Old Navy, Bed Bath & Beyond, and Burlington will be replaced with WSHP RTUs operating in single-zone VAV mode.  â€¢	VAV RTUs for Marshalls will be replaced with WSHP RTUs serving VAVs with electric reheat.  â€¢	All equipment is to be fully controlled and monitored via BMS.  â€¢	Additional 538-Ton 2 Cell 15 HP fan cooling tower is installed for additional tenant WSHP load. â€¢	Electric heat pump boilers are utilized in the calculation.  â€¢	Existing 2-pipe HW/CHW supply and return piping riser from the penthouse down to the ground/2nd level vacant tenants can be utilized for heat pump loop supply/return piping. â€¢	Existing air source VRF for the former IKEA space will be utilized for cooling/heating of spaces served by new tenant. To be Further Evaluated / Analyzed:  The largest consideration of the electrification conversion is the current electrical load of the facility and the required electrical service needed to support new equipment.  The building owner is encouraged to seek a MEP engineering surveyor to determine the current electrical capacity, determine the increase in electrical capacity needed due to proposed mechanical systems upgrades, and the implementation costs as well as the life-cycle costs associated with the utility increasing the capacity and the facilities demand increasing from the new systems. In addition, the occupancy of the facility heavily drives the potential energy savings of this measure. The occupancy schedule in an energy savings calculation should be coordinated and discussed with the ownership team to best reflect a future tenantsâ€™ operating hours.

column1593: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment radiators.  TRVs automatically regulate the steam flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing steam flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing steam flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant.

column1446: Cooling in this building is utilizing window AC units. Some of the tenants keep the AC units on the window during heating season. Heat escapes from the gaps at windows, over load the heating system and increase the heating cost directly. In addition, it create draft in the apartments and reduce the indoor comfort. We recommend remove all window AC units from windows during heating season. We understand that some window ACs may belong to tenants. If tenants do not want to remove them, installing window AC covers can be an alternative solution.

column1455: Based on field observations many units have high flow rate fixtures that can be upgraded. Replacing water fixtures with low-flowing fixtures is the most cost-effective water conservation measures. Aerating showerheads and aerators are inexpensive devices that can be installed to tenant units. These fixtures mix air with water, forming a misty spray. We recommend 1.5 gpm low flow aerators to kitchen sinks and bathroom sinks, and 2.0 gpm low flow showerhead to existing showers.
column1464: Currently all lights in common area, include basement hallways, stairways and common floors, are kept on 24 hours per day seven days per week. Due to the safety, lights in hallways and common areas cannot be shut off. But most lights can be dimmed. Installing dimmable sensor will allow lights to operate at a lower wattage, usually at 60% of full wattage, depending on the package selected. Each sensor costs approximately $79.5. We assume existing light bulbs are can be dimmed without upgrade.

column1446: Linear fluorescent lamps, incandescent, compact fluorescent, and some LED lamps were observed in common areas including the building lobby, stairwells, hallways, mechanical rooms, and exterior.  Replacement of the less efficient lighting types with higher efficiency LED lighting options will provide immediate energy savings and reduced operating costs.

column1495: During the heating season, Energy Recovery Ventilators (ERVs) installed in front of outdoor air intakes pre-temper cold outdoor air via heat transfer from warmer exhaust air.  During the cooling season, this effect is reversed as hot outdoor air is pre-tempered via heat transfer to cooler exhaust air. This pre-tempering of intake air reduces the overall load on building heating and/or cooling systems that are responsible for conditioning the intake air.  ERVs may be selected that do not mix exhaust air and intake air in any manner, thereby eliminating any concern over odors or contamination of intake air. The rooftop packaged units serving common area hallways are in close proximity to several exhaust fans and therefore a good candidate for installation of an ERV unit.  As the rooftop unit is used for both heating and cooling, installation of an ERV will effectively lower overall building heating and cooling costs. Duct exhaust air from the rooftop exhausts to an ERV.  The ERV will then provide pre-tempered outdoor air to the rooftop package units.  The size of the ERV must be properly matched to the intake air requirements of the rooftop unit.  One or more exhaust flows may be connected to the ERV up to the maximum capacity of the ERV.  Increasing the amount of exhaust air captured will increase overall efficiency gains and result in greater energy savings.

column1544: Three (3) 15HP motors [2 active, 1 standby] are used to provide domestic water pressure to the building.  These motors are standard efficiency motors that are past their useful life (15+ years).  Premium efficiency motors currently available would decrease the electricity used for pumping domestic water. Retrofit existing pump motors with NEMA premium efficiency motors. For all motors, premium efficiency motor converts more power input into useful work compared to a standard efficiency motor of this age.
column1593: The current two (2) heating hot water heat injection boilers (BOI1 and BOI2) are standard efficiency non-condensing models.  Installation of a new condensing systems will result in improved combustion efficiency and lower operating costs. Replace the existing two (2) heating hot water heat injection boilers with high efficiency, condensing boilers.

column1446: Cooling in this building is utilizing window AC units. Some of the tenants keep the AC units on the window during heating season. Heat escapes from the gaps at windows, over load the heating system and increase the heating cost directly. In addition, it create draft in the apartments and reduce the indoor comfort. We recommend remove all window AC units from windows during heating season. We understand that some window ACs may belong to tenants. If tenants do not want to remove them, installing window AC covers can be an alternative solution.
column1455: Based on field observations many units have high flow rate fixtures that can be upgraded. Replacing water fixtures with low-flowing fixtures is the most cost-effective water conservation measures. Aerating showerheads and aerators are inexpensive devices that can be installed to tenant units. These fixtures mix air with water, forming a misty spray. We recommend 1.5 gpm low flow aerators to kitchen sinks and bathroom sinks, and 2.0 gpm low flow showerhead to existing showers. The savings estimate assumes only the estimated percentage of the showers/sinks are replaced by low flow devices. The cost estimates are based on the time it will take for building staff to un-install existing showerheads/aerators, re-install new low flow devices, as well as repairing associated piping damage when needed.

column1464: Existing boiler is utilizing only 1 temperature sensor and 1 outdoor sensor. Indoor temperature in apartments are not monitored. We recommend install advanced control which includes indoor temperature sensors and programmable function. This measure will reduce the heating system temperature set point to 70F or lower. Reducing heating system temperature set point will reduce utility cost directly. In addition, it reduces heating load and extends heating system life.

column1446: Two (2) 3/4HP pumps are used to supply domestic hot water throughout the building. These motors operate 24/7.  All of the motors are standard efficiency motors. Retrofit existing fan motors with ECM motors. ECM motors are significantly more efficient compared to standard efficiency motors and operate at significantly lower temperatures. Additionally, these motors have extended motor life and are lower maintenance costs than the existing traditional induction motors.
column1490: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1491: Install a Dedicated Domestic Hot Water Heater
column1495: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Install a dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boiler.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 80% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, this dedicated unit will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.

column1544: The water source heat pumps in the super's office, elevator motor room, gym, and lobby are older units, and are operating at reduced efficiencies.  Direct replacement with modern, high efficiency system would result in lower energy consumption, improved system reliability, and reduced overall operating costs. Replace these older units with new equipment with premium efficiency ratings.  The incremental cost of premium efficiency equipment is directly offset by ongoing reduction in energy consumption.

column1491: Install VFD on Condenser Water Pumps
column1495: The closed condenser water distribution system in the building is currently a constant flow system that operates continuously to supply condenser water to water source heat pumps throughout the building.  The majority of observed heat pump units were fitted with 3-way valves that bypass condenser water flow when the unit is shut off. Demand for condenser water varies greatly based on the cooling load, heating load, and occupancy of the building.  During unoccupied hours and shoulder months, most heat pump units will be bypassing condenser water flow.  Although there is minimal need for condenser water during these times, the use of bypass valves means that the pump is still circulating condenser water at full speed.  This situation results in wasted pump energy during periods of low cooling demand. Variable flow condenser water systems vary the pump speed in response to actual condenser water demand.  In these systems, bypass valves are replaced with 2-way (on/off) valves and a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) is used to control the pump speed.  As heat pump units shut off and the 2-way valves close, pressure within the circulating system increases.  The VFD responds to this pressure increase by slowing the pump motor.  This reduction in motor speed provides significant energy savings. Install VFDs on the closed loop water pump to optimize pump speed based on actual load conditions.  Any 3-way bypass valves must also be replaced with 2-way on/off valves on all water source heat pumps serviced by the closed water loop.

column1495: This measure is applied by installing insulated radiator covers with integrated temperature controls and sensors. column1446: It is recommended that the existing Rooftop Units are equipped with integrated demand-controlled ventilation (DCV), a multi-variable speed fan, and a dual enthalpy air-side economizer. DCV systems determine occupancy using a CO2 sensor and reduce heating and cooling loads by modulating outdoor air intake to meet ventilation requirements. Multi/variable speed fan motors reduce the fan speed for first stage cooling and ventilation. Air-side economizers reduce mechanical cooling requirements by supplying outside air to the space when the outside air meets conditions deemed suitable for cooling.

It is recommended that these units reach their Useful Life limit they are replaced with Energy Recovery Ventilators. ERVs reduce heating and cooling loads while maintaining required ventilation rates by facilitating heat transfer between outgoing conditioned air and incoming outdoor air. ERVs employ air-to-air heat exchangers to recover energy from exhaust air for the purpose of pre-conditioning outdoor air prior to supplying the conditioned air to the space directly. Calculations assume that ERVs are of type that transfer both sensible and latent heat between supply and exhaust airstreams.

column1446: Cooling in this building is utilizing window AC units. Some of the tenants keep the AC units on the window during heating season. Heat escapes from the gaps at windows, over load the heating system and increase the heating cost directly. In addition, it create draft in the apartments and reduce the indoor comfort. We recommend remove all window AC units from windows during heating season. We understand that some window ACs may belong to tenants. If tenants do not want to remove them, installing window AC covers can be an alternative solution.

column1455: Based on field observations many units have high flow rate fixtures that can be upgraded. Replacing water fixtures with low-flowing fixtures is the most cost-effective water conservation measures. Aerating showerheads and aerators are inexpensive devices that can be installed to tenant units. These fixtures mix air with water, forming a misty spray. We recommend 1.5 gpm low flow aerators to kitchen sinks and bathroom sinks, and 2.0 gpm low flow showerhead to existing showers.
column1464: Currently all lights in common area, include basement hallways, stairways and common floors, are kept on 24 hours per day seven days per week. Due to the safety, lights in hallways and common areas cannot be shut off. But most lights can be dimmed. Installing dimmable sensor will allow lights to operate at a lower wattage, usually at 60% of full wattage, depending on the package selected. Each sensor costs approximately $79.5. We assume existing light bulbs are can be dimmed without upgrade.

column1442: Install VFDs on Condenser Water Pumps
column1446: The condenser water distribution system in the building is currently a constant flow system that operates continuously to supply condenser water to water source heat pumps throughout the building.  The majority of observed heat pump units were fitted with 3-way valves that bypass condenser water flow when the unit is shut off. Demand for condenser water varies greatly based on the cooling load, heating load, and occupancy of the building.  During unoccupied hours, most water source heat pump units will be bypassing condenser water flow.  Although there is minimal need for condenser water during these times, the use of bypass valves means that the pump is still circulating condenser water at full speed.  This situation results in wasted pump energy during periods of low cooling and heating demand. Variable flow condenser water systems vary the pump speed in response to actual condenser water demand.  In these systems, bypass valves are replaced with 2-way (on/off) valves and a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) is used to control the pump speed.  As water source heat pumps shut off and the 2-way valves close, pressure within the circulating system increases.  The VFD responds to this pressure increase by slowing the pump motor.  This reduction in motor speed provides significant energy savings. Install VFDs on each of the condenser water pumps to optimize pump speed based on actual condenser water load.  All 3-way bypass valves must also be replaced with 2-way on/off valves on all water cooled air conditioning systems serviced by the heating water loop.  In addition, pump motors will need to be replaced with premium efficiency models as required for VFD compatibility.
column1490: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1491: Install VFDs on Heating Hot Water Pumps
column1495: The heating water closed loop system is currently a constant flow system that operates continuously to supply  water to hot water radiators throughout the building. Demand for heating water varies greatly based on the loads and occupancy of the building.  During unoccupied hours and  shoulder seasons, most units will be bypassing water flow.  Although there is minimal need for heating water during these times, this type of system means that the pump is still circulating water at full speed.  This situation results in wasted pump energy during periods of low demand. Variable flow water systems vary the pump speed in response to actual demand.  In these systems, bypass valves are replaced with 2-way (on/off) valves as needed and a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) is used to control the pump speed.  As hot water radiators shut off and the 2-way valves close, pressure within the circulating system increases.  The VFD responds to this pressure increase by slowing the pump motor.  This reduction in motor speed provides significant energy savings. Install VFDs on the closed loop water pump to optimize pump speed based on actual load conditions.  Any 3-way bypass valves must also be replaced with 2-way on/off valves on all radiators serviced by the closed water loop.  In addition, pump motors will need to be replaced with premium efficiency models as required for VFD compatibility.

column1544: Linear fluorescent lamps, incandescent, compact fluorescent, and LED lamps were observed in common areas including the building lobby, stairwells, hallways, mechanical rooms, and exterior.  Replacement of the less efficient lighting types with higher efficiency LED lighting options will provide immediate energy savings and reduced operating costs.
column1593: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Install a dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boiler.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 84% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, this dedicated unit will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.

column1491: Install VFD on Condenser Water Pump
column1495: The closed condenser water distribution system in the building is currently a constant flow system that operates continuously to supply condenser water to water source heat pumps throughout the building.  The majority of observed heat pump units were fitted with 3-way valves that bypass condenser water flow when the unit is shut off.Demand for condenser water varies greatly based on the cooling load, heating load, and occupancy of the building.  During unoccupied hours and shoulder months, most heat pump units will be bypassing condenser water flow.  Although there is minimal need for condenser water during these times, the use of bypass valves means that the pump is still circulating condenser water at full speed.  This situation results in wasted pump energy during periods of low cooling demand. Variable flow condenser water systems vary the pump speed in response to actual condenser water demand.  In these systems, bypass valves are replaced with 2-way (on/off) valves and a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) is used to control the pump speed.  As heat pump units shut off and the 2-way valves close, pressure within the circulating system increases.  The VFD responds to this pressure increase by slowing the pump motor.  This reduction in motor speed provides significant energy savings.

column1442: Install a Dedicated Domestic Hot Water Heater
column1446: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Install a dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boiler.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 84% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, this dedicated unit will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.
column1490: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1495: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment fan coil units.  TRVs automatically regulate the heating water flow to the fan coil units based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing water flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing water flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.

column1544: During the site survey, un-insulated condensate pipes less than 3" in diameter were observed in unconditioned spaces.  Un-insulated pipes in unconditioned spaces lead to significant thermal energy loss and cause related HVAC systems to operate with increased frequency and longer run times.  Insulating these pipes and all associated fittings in accordance with the New York City Energy Conservation Code (NYCECC) will minimize these thermal losses. Insulate all condensate pipes less than 3" in diameter in unconditioned spaces in accordance with the NYCECC.  All associated fittings such as elbows, valves, couplings, etc. experience heat loss and should be insulated as well.

column1495: The dual-temperature pumps in the Boiler Room are currently constant speed, manually rotated, and operate in a lead/lag configuration 24/7. column1504: The existing heat control system operates based on the Hot Water Supply temperature, maintaining the loop at 150F. column1513: SWA observed that the current DHW system does not have a mixing valve, and often delivers water at temperatures as high as 150F. column1446: Insulating steam pipes in a garage area involves wrapping the pipes with insulating material to minimize heat loss during transport. column1495: Installing Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) on steam boiler radiators involves attaching TRVs to each individual radiator. TRVs function by sensing the temperature of the room and adjusting the flow of steam into the radiator accordingly. When the desired temperature is reached, the valve closes partially or completely, regulating the amount of heat emitted by the radiator. This process helps maintain a consistent temperature throughout the space while preventing overheating.

By dynamically controlling heating output, STRE systems ensure rooms remain at desired temperatures without wasteful overheating.

column1446: Based on field observations many units have high flow rate fixtures that can be upgraded. Replacing water fixtures with low-flowing fixtures is the most cost-effective water conservation measures. Aerating showerheads and aerators are inexpensive devices that can be installed to tenant units. These fixtures mix air with water, forming a misty spray. We recommend 1.5 gpm low flow aerators to kitchen sinks and bathroom sinks, and 2.0 gpm low flow showerhead to existing showers. The savings estimate assumes only the estimated percentage of the showers/sinks are replaced by low flow devices. The cost estimates are based on the time it will take for building staff to un-install existing showerheads/aerators, re-install new low flow devices, as well as repairing associated piping damage when needed.

column1544: Installing Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) on hot water (HW) pumps and booster pumps is a crucial energy efficiency measure. VFDs adjust the motor speed of these pumps to match the system's demand, reducing energy consumption and operational costs. By allowing the pumps to operate at variable speeds rather than a constant full speed, VFDs enhance system performance, prolong equipment life, and decrease wear and tear.
column1593: Installing solar panels on a roof is a process that enhances energy efficiency by harnessing the sun's renewable energy. These panels absorb sunlight and convert it into electricity through photovoltaic cells. An inverter then converts this DC electricity into AC electricity, which can power appliances and devices in the building. Any excess electricity generated can be stored in batteries for later use or fed back into the grid for credits. Overall, this process not only reduces reliance on traditional energy sources but also lowers energy bills and carbon footprint, contributing to a more sustainable future.

column1446: During the heating season, Energy Recovery Ventilators (ERVs) installed in front of outdoor air intakes pre-temper cold outdoor air via heat transfer from warmer exhaust air.  During the cooling season, this effect is reversed as hot outdoor air is pre-tempered via heat transfer to cooler exhaust air. This pre-tempering of intake air reduces the overall load on building heating and/or cooling systems that are responsible for conditioning the intake air.  ERVs may be selected that do not mix exhaust air and intake air in any manner, thereby eliminating any concern over odors or contamination of intake air.The rooftop packaged unit serving common area hallways is in close proximity to several exhaust fans and therefore a good candidate for installation of an ERV unit.  As the rooftop unit is used for both heating and cooling, installation of an ERV will effectively lower overall building heating and cooling costs.

column1446: Currently all lights in common area, include basement hallways, stairways and common floors, are kept on 24 hours per day seven days per week. Due to the safety, lights in hallways and common areas cannot be shut off. But most lights can be dimmed. Installing dimmable sensor will allow lights to operate at a lower wattage, usually at 60% of full wattage, depending on the package selected. Each sensor costs approximately $79.5. We assume existing light bulbs are can be dimmed without upgrade.
column1455: Cooling in this building is utilizing window AC units. Some of the tenants keep the AC units on the window during heating season. Heat escapes from the gaps at windows, over load the heating system and increase the heating cost directly. In addition, it create draft in the apartments and reduce the indoor comfort. We recommend remove all window AC units from windows during heating season. We understand that some window ACs may belong to tenants. If tenants do not want to remove them, installing window AC covers can be an alternative solution.
column1464: Based on field observations many units have high flow rate fixtures that can be upgraded. Replacing water fixtures with low-flowing fixtures is the most cost-effective water conservation measures. Aerating showerheads and aerators are inexpensive devices that can be installed to tenant units. These fixtures mix air with water, forming a misty spray. We recommend 1.5 gpm low flow aerators to kitchen sinks and bathroom sinks, and 2.0 gpm low flow showerhead to existing showers. The savings estimate assumes only the estimated percentage of the showers/sinks are replaced by low flow devices. The cost estimates are based on the time it will take for building staff to un-install existing showerheads/aerators, re-install new low flow devices, as well as repaire associated piping damage when needed.

column1455: Existing Conditions: During the site visits, it was noted that several locations of hot water piping in Target was missing insulation. Heat loss to the environment via uninsulated piping is reducing the efficiency of heating via the hot water coils in the water cooled AC units.  Recommendation: Lilker recommends insulating the hot water piping and trim that is currently bare to maximize the efficiency of the heating hot water system.
