column1495: Existing Condition The facility currently operates the condenser water system at a constant primary loop supply temperature setpoint of 74Â°F. The differential pressure setpoint is at 16 PSI with one secondary pump maintaining the setpoint during the site visit. The building engineer noted that two pumps are almost never necessary to maintain the pressure setpoint.  In addition, it was observed that the primary condenser water pumps operate at variable speed based on cooling demand and run at minimum speed when the cooling towers are de-energized. On a call for cooling to meet the primary temperature setpoint, the following sequence occurs from the cooling towers being de-energized: â€¢	Both cooling towers energize at minimum fan speed. â€¢	Once the BMS calculates that this will not be enough cooling to meet the setpoint, the lag cooling tower de-energizes, and the lead towerâ€™s fan is allowed to modulate speed.  â€¢	Once lead cooling towerâ€™s fan reached 100% speed, the lag cooling tower energized and modulated speed to 100%.  â€¢	This sequence occurred over 45 minutes due to the slow fan ramp time not meeting the cooling needs, resulting in only one cooling tower operating for 30 minutes and the primary water temperature reaching a maximum of 84Â°F.  Recommendation  Lilker recommends the following steps to optimize and re-balance the condenser water system:  â€¢	Reprogram the condenser water system to control to a secondary water temperature setpoint that is automatically reset based on the current outdoor air wet bulb temperature plus cooling tower approach (Approx. 7Â°F). Implement a minimum setpoint of 65Â°F and a maximum setpoint of 85Â°F.  â€¢	Fully rebalance the condenser water system. This will include a balancer adjusting the primary and secondary systems to deliver the design flow, and re-setting the DP setpoint at the DP reading when all valves are open and pumps are at 100%. â€¢	Reprogram the condenser water system to modify the sequence described above in the existing condition section. On a call for cooling, one tower and one pump energize and the cooling tower fan and primary pump ramp together toward maximum speed to meet the secondary condenser water supply temperature setpoint. Once at 100% for an adjustable amount of time, the lag tower fan and second primary pump energize at minimum and ramp towards maximum to meet the setpoint. Reverse sequence occurs upon the supply temperature dropping below the setpoint. Benefits and Energy Savings: 1.	By controlling to a secondary setpoint that is automatically reset based on OA temperature, the best energy efficiency is maintained both at the cooling tower fan and at the downstream HVAC units. As condenser water supply temperature decreases, the unitsâ€™ compressors will not have to work as hard to achieve the same amount of cooling.   2.	This will increase the effective life of the main condenser water system equipment as a result of the reduced runtime on the cooling tower fans and primary/secondary pumps.    Implementation Considerations: 1.	All downstream HVAC and refrigeration units utilizing condenser water will need to be verified to be operable down to the minimum 65Â°F supply setpoint.
column1504: Existing Condition The facility currently operates the condenser water system 24/7 due to the Target space containing water cooled refrigeration for food and beverage cases in the store floor as well as walk-in storage. As a result, the pumps run continuously during the nights and in winter.  Recommendation  Lilker recommends utilizing a new small condenser water system that ties into existing piping for the 24/7 refrigeration at Target:  â€¢	Install a new closed circuit cooler and two variable volume pumps (Lead/Standby) on the roof for the Target that will operate at night and throughout the winter for water cooled refrigeration needs. System and pump shall be sized for refrigeration needs and unoccupied space cooling as required.  â€¢	Enable the occupancy schedule of the main condenser water plant for 7AM â€“ 11PM during store open hours. Winterize the main condenser water system during the heating season.  â€¢	Install isolation valves on the main CW plant supply and return to Target and new dedicated system to isolate the systems. â€¢	Integrate new condenser water system into the BMS.  â€¢	Balance the pumps as follows: Set pump minimum speed with all refrigeration valves open for 24/7 cooling, and all water cooled AC valves closed. Set pump maximum speed with all water cooled AC and refrigeration valves open. Modulate in between based on flow needs for unoccupied / winter cooling.   Benefits and Energy Savings: 2.	By shutting down the main condenser water plant during nights and in the winter when only the Target refrigeration equipment needs condenser water, cooling tower fan energy and pumping energy is reduced due to smaller motors being required on the dedicated system.  3.	This will increase the effective life of the main condenser water system equipment as a result of the reduced runtime on the cooling tower fans and primary/secondary pumps.  4.	By isolating the Target space with the dedicated system, the main condenser system can still be energized as needed for unoccupied / winter cooling in the other retail spaces.   Implementation Considerations: 1.	Water Treatment: The new dedicated system will bypass the main condenser loop chemical shot feeder. An additional unit may need to be installed for proper water treatment.
column1512: Convert CV system to VAV system
column1513: Existing Condition The large water cooled AC units with hot water coils in H&M and Burlington currently operate as constant volume units controlling to space temperature. During all occupied store hours, the fans run at constant speed to deliver outside ventilation air that is supplied by OAFs near the return air inlets for the units in mechanical rooms.  Recommendation  Lilker recommends retrofitting the units with variable frequency drives to operate the units as Single-Zone Variable Air Volume units (SZVAVs): â€¢	Install VFDs for the eight 20 ton and two 12.5 ton units in Burlington, and the five 25 ton and one 10 ton unit in H&M.  â€¢	When the space temperature setpoints are satisfied, operate the supply fans at 50% speed to reduce fan energy but still deliver ventilation air to the space.  â€¢	When heating or cooling is required, modulate the fan speed between 50 and 100% speed based on the differential between current space temperature and setpoint.  â€¢	Integrate new VFDs and control strategy into tenant Building Management System as required.  Benefits and Energy Savings: 1.	By reducing the fan speed, the energy usage reduction follows the fan affinity laws where power is proportional to the cube of the fan speed.  2.	Variable volume configuration with VFDs are options under the Carrier and Johnson Controls unit model types present in Burlington and H&M.

column1446: Installing Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) on domestic water booster pumps enhances energy  efficiency by optimizing pump speed according to real-time demand. This measure reduces energy  consumption and wear on the pump, leading to lower operational costs and extended equipment  lifespan. VFDs adjust the motor speed to match water usage, preventing unnecessary energy use  during periods of low demand. Additionally, this improvement contributes to a more sustainable  building operation by reducing overall energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions.

column1495: Replacing the rooftop unit (RTU) with advanced RTU controls that incorporate Demand Control  Ventilation (DCV) optimizes energy efficiency by adjusting the ventilation rates based on  occupancy levels. This smart control system reduces unnecessary heating and cooling, leading to  significant energy savings. By monitoring CO2 levels, the system ensures that fresh air is supplied  only when needed, improving indoor air quality. Overall, this upgrade enhances comfort while  minimizing operational costs.

column1544: Installing air source heat pumps in common areas improves energy efficiency by utilizing outdoor  air to provide heating and cooling, significantly reducing energy consumption compared to  traditional systems. These pumps transfer heat instead of generating it, making them a highly  efficient option, especially in moderate climates. They offer year-round comfort by reversing the  process for cooling in summer and heating in winter. This upgrade leads to lower utility costs and  reduced greenhouse gas emissions.

column1446: During the site survey, un-insulated domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter were observed in unconditioned spaces.  Un-insulated pipes in unconditioned spaces lead to significant thermal energy loss and cause related HVAC systems to operate with increased frequency and longer run times. Insulate all domestic hot water pipes less than 3" in diameter in unconditioned spaces in accordance with the NYCECC.  All associated fittings such as elbows, valves, couplings, etc. experience heat loss and should be insulated as well.

column1495: Linear fluorescent lamps, compact fluorescent, Incandescent, High Pressure Sodium, and LED lamps were observed in common areas including the building lobby, stairwells, hallways, mechanical rooms, and exterior.  Replacement of the less efficient lighting types with higher efficiency LED lighting options will provide immediate energy savings and reduced operating costs.
column1539: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1544: Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs) are temperature responsive valves that replace the manual on/off valves currently installed on apartment radiators. TRVs automatically regulate the heating water flow to the radiators based on actual space conditions.  As the space heats up, the TRV will close, reducing water flow to the terminal unit.  As the space cools down, the TRV will open, allowing water flow to the terminal unit.  This thermostatic control reduces space overheating and reduces overall heating energy consumption.   TRVs are adjustable such that space temperatures can be generally controlled by the space occupant. Replace all terminal unit on/off valves with Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs).  TRVs with remote control units are recommended to better enable occupant control.
column1589: Install a Dedicated Domestic Hot Water Heater
column1593: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) is currently produced via immersion coil heat exchangers installed in the central steam boiler.  This system is relatively inefficient as compared to dedicated DHW equipment and may result in unnecessary firing of the steam boilers to satisfy DHW loads when heating is not necessary (e.g. during shoulder seasons). Currently, installation of dedicated DHW boilers is not economically feasible. However, if costs were to decrease in the future, it is recommended that management re-investigate the installation of dedicated Natural Gas fired fully condensing Domestic Hot Water boilers.  Fully condensing DHW boilers have efficiencies approaching 98% as compared to 84% for the central steam boiler.  In addition, the dedicated units will eliminate any unnecessary firing of the steam boiler when heating is not necessary.

column1446: CodeGreen recommends installing occupancy sensors to control the lighting in the boiler room and EMR. Bi-level dimming controls should be implemented for the LED fixtures in the stairwells. Daylight sensors can be installed to control the lighting in the lobby. Occupancy sensors save energy by turning lights on automatically when someone enters a room, and save energy by turning lights off soon after the last occupant has left the room. Bi-level lighting control provide two levels of "on" in addition to "off". Best application is for stairwells and other common areas where certain level of lighting foot candles have to be delivered per the code requirements. Daylight sensors can be implemented in the lobby as they can automatically dim lights when enough daylight is present.
column1455: CodeGreen recommends converting from fuel oil #4 to natural gas to operate the boilers. Natural gas is approximately one-half the cost of fuel oil factoring in the lower heating content. Additional benefits of the gas are that the boiler maintenance would be reduced since gas burns cleaner than oil, and the oil storage tank could be removed. As the current burner is well maintained and utilizes natural gas for pilot lighting, converting from fuel oil #4 to natural gas may not require new burners. However, few burner components will need to be replaced and this is a cost effective short term alternative as the cost to replace these boilers with comparable new steam boilers would be very expensive. This will achieve the goal to switch to gas fired boiler. To implement this ECM, the gas service to the building would need to be verified to be able to transport the required volume and pressure of gas for the new burners.
column1464: CodeGreen recommends installing a low-e film on the windows located on the south and east facade as a measure to reduce energy losses due to inefficient windows. Adding low-e film on the windows, will help reduce overall HVAC expenses due to heating and cooling losses. In addition, insulated window film will also increase interior comfort while lowering your overall energy costs.
column1490: Potential Capital Recommendations
column1495: While the VRF system increases system efficiency, it is not feasible to eliminate the steam distribution system. This means that this measure may add equipment to maintain and increase the complexity of the HVAC system at the building. Additionally, modification to the heating plant by converting to hydronic system and then using a "air to water heat pump" will be a capital intensive project. Because VRF technology is rapidly advancing and the expected useful lifetime (EUL) of the existing equipment warrants waiting to proceed with this measure (all installed in 2000). The building is also within the NYC's GHG limits as specified by the Climate Mobilization Act (CMA), it is assumed that this ECM will not be implemented by the building for at least 15 more years. An assessment of the feasibility of retrofiting the existing AHU's with refrigerant based coils should be conducted prior to proceeding with this ECM. The proposed plan could serve as an interim source of  heating for the building until such time as better permanent solutions (i.e. large commercial scale air-cooled heat pumps) can become readily available.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           The existing fuel oil fired boiler has a output capacity of 6,695 MBH. This capacity satisfies the whole building heating requirements. Therefore, it is recommended to install the electric boiler(s) of similar capacity. For this measure, (1) Lochinvar BW*36 boiler has been proposed,  rated at 7,063 MBH capacity. This plant option provides for the most straightforward equipment replacement. The equipment chosen are traditional and market ready equipment that can be installed immediately. This design allows for the immediate use of electricity as the primary source of heating. The use of electric boilers will require a significant upgrade in the electrical service to the building. From a plant operations and maintenance perspective, this solution will result in cost increases to the maintenance of the electric boilers and the systems supporting the additional electrical infrastructure.
